articles.title: Rochdale primary schools launch engineering programme for pupils
articles.excerpt: Ten primary schools in Rochdale have begun a new engineering initiative to inspire students through hands-on learning and professional interaction.
articles.content_html:
Ten primary schools in Rochdale have launched a new initiative aimed at inspiring the next generation of engineers through hands-on learning. Staff from these schools participated in a continuous professional development (CPD) training day to implement the Primary Engineer Vehicle Programme.

The programme allows pupils to build and test their own vehicle models while interacting with engineering professionals. At the end of the programme, students will celebrate their achievements at a joint school event, showcasing their projects.

Rochdale Council, in partnership with Rochdale Development and Primary Engineers, is facilitating this initiative. The programme includes a full day of CPD training, high-quality kits, and classroom resources, enabling 60 pupils at each school to construct 15 shoebox locomotives and 15 motorised locomotives.

This year marks the first collaboration between these organisations, with the aim of fostering interest in STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) subjects among young learners in Rochdale.

articles.title: Marios Plus Pizzeria rated 1 out of 5 for food hygiene
articles.excerpt: Marios Plus Pizzeria, a takeaway or sandwich shop at 8 Wood Street, Middleton, Manchester, M24 5TF, has been given a food hygiene rating of 1 out of 5, meaning major improvement is necessary, after an inspection on 20 October 2026.
articles.content_html:
Marios Plus Pizzeria, a takeaway or sandwich shop at 8 Wood Street, Middleton, Manchester, M24 5TF, has been given a food hygiene rating of 1 out of 5, meaning major improvement is necessary, after an inspection on 20 October 2026.

The rating appears on the Food Standards Agency's public register for the Rochdale borough, checked by Rochdale Daily on 27 November 2026. A low rating is usually published only after the business's 21-day appeal period has passed, so it appears some weeks after the inspection.

Under the national Food Hygiene Rating Scheme, councils score businesses from 0, where urgent improvement is necessary, to 5, where hygiene standards are very good.

The score reflects how food was handled, the condition of the premises and how food safety was managed on the day of the inspection. It is not a judgement of the quality of the food.

64 food businesses in the borough currently hold a rating of 0 or 1, according to the same register.

A business can appeal its rating, publish a right of reply alongside it on the Food Standards Agency website, and ask for a re-inspection once improvements have been made, so the rating may since have changed. The current rating is at https://ratings.food.gov.uk/business/802265.

articles.title: NHS asks Rochdale families to help get patients home safely from hospital this winter
articles.excerpt: Families and friends are being asked to be ready to collect loved ones, prepare their homes and speak to ward teams early as North West NHS services work to get patients home sooner.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale families are being asked to help relatives leave hospital safely this winter as North West NHS services work to get patients home sooner.

NHS England says hospitals and community services across the region are working to make sure patients can leave hospital as soon as they are well enough. Families and friends can help by being ready to collect their loved ones when the time comes.

Returning to familiar surroundings with the right support in place can help people recover, regain their independence and get back to their usual routines. Staying in hospital longer than needed can increase the risk of infection and loss of strength and mobility.

Dr Michael Gregory, Regional Medical Director for NHS England in the North West, said: “For patients, going home is about getting back to the people and everyday life they know. This is something that can make a real difference to recovery. Families and friends can help make a difference by helping their loved ones take that next step.

“If you are worried about how someone will manage, please speak to the ward team early. We want to understand those concerns and what help you can offer, so we can plan together for a safe return home.”

Ward teams will work with patients and, where appropriate, their family, friends or unpaid carers to plan a safe discharge. They will discuss what support may be available and how to access it, and will aim for discharge earlier in the day where possible.

Before leaving, patients and those supporting them should understand the discharge plan, including any medicines, follow-up appointments and who to contact with concerns.

NHS England suggests families and friends check the expected discharge date and time with the ward team, and help arrange transport where possible.

Relatives can bring suitable clothes and shoes for the journey home, and check with the ward that medicines are ready and that their loved one understands how to take them.

At home, families can help by putting the heating on, making sure food and other essentials are available, and clearing walkways of clutter and trip hazards.

They should also make sure the patient knows who to contact if they need help.

Across the North West, specialist wards and services providing hospital-level care at home are helping patients leave hospital sooner. They include the Oasis Unit at Rochdale Infirmary, a specialist dementia ward featured in the same NHS England campaign.

Anyone who needs urgent medical help after returning home and is unsure where to turn can contact NHS 111 by phone or at 111.nhs.uk. For a life-threatening emergency, call 999.

Source: NHS England North West press office, press release issued on 24 November 2026.

What it means for Rochdale families

  • Families can check the expected discharge date and time with the ward team, and help arrange transport where possible.
  • Relatives can check with the ward that medicines are ready and that their loved one understands how to take them.
  • Anyone who needs urgent medical help after returning home and is unsure where to turn can contact NHS 111 by phone or at 111.nhs.uk.

articles.content_html:
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) have issued an urgent appeal for information regarding a missing 16-year-old boy named Michael from Rochdale. He was last seen on Dale Road in Middleton at around 3pm on Thursday, 26 November 2026.

Police are becoming increasingly concerned for Michael's welfare and want to ensure he is safe. He is described as 5ft 3in tall, of medium build, with dark brown hair that is fluffy on top.

At the time of his disappearance, he was wearing a black puffer jacket, turquoise trail berg pants, and black On Cloud trainers. Michael also has a scar on his forehead.

In a post on their Rochdale Facebook page, GMP stated that Michael is known to frequent Salford Quays and the surrounding areas. They are urging anyone with information about his whereabouts to contact them.

Police are committed to locating Michael as quickly as possible.

articles.title: Rochdale Infirmary dementia care scheme cuts hospital stays by up to eight days
articles.excerpt: Specialist dementia wards including Rochdale Infirmary’s Oasis Unit are helping patients return home sooner, with average stays reduced by up to eight days.
articles.content_html:
A specialist dementia care model used at Rochdale Infirmary is helping patients return home sooner, with average hospital stays across the programme reduced by up to eight days, NHS England says.

The Oasis Unit at Rochdale Infirmary is one of three Northern Care Alliance services highlighted in a winter discharge campaign. Similar specialist dementia wards operate at Fairfield General Hospital in Bury and Salford Royal.

Patients living with dementia can remain on the same ward throughout their hospital stay, reducing moves that can be unsettling and allowing staff to provide care in a familiar environment. Activities are tailored to individual needs as part of the approach.

Northern Care Alliance information describes the Oasis Unit as a 10-bed medical ward for patients who have an acute medical condition and are also living with dementia. The unit includes colour-coordinated rooms and shared spaces designed to help with orientation and recovery.

NHS England said teams begin speaking with relatives early in a patient's stay and work with Age UK to arrange support for a safe return home. Across the specialist ward programme, the average length of stay has fallen by up to eight days.

Dr Michael Gregory, NHS England's Regional Medical Director for the North West, said: “Families and friends can help make a difference by helping their loved ones take that next step.”

The NHS is asking relatives and carers to discuss practical arrangements with hospital teams before a patient is ready to leave. This can include transport, suitable clothing, food at home and help with follow-up appointments or medicines.

For Rochdale families, early discharge planning can reduce delays once a patient is medically ready to leave hospital and make the move home safer.

Sources: NHS England North West news release, 24 November 2026; Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust, Oasis Unit patient information and Discharge Integration Frontrunner Programme.

articles.title: First Bus Rochdale wins national Gold for Routes to Work scheme
articles.excerpt: First Bus Rochdale’s employability programme has won Gold at the UK Bus Awards after helping local young people build skills and move into work.
articles.content_html:
First Bus Rochdale’s Routes to Work programme has won Gold in the Bus and the Community category at the 2026 UK Bus Awards, adding to the operator’s Community Engagement Award at the Rochdale Business Awards.

The national winners were announced in London on Tuesday 24 November. The UK Bus Awards named Routes to Work as the Gold winner ahead of schemes from First Bus West Yorkshire and Arriva Merseyside.

Routes to Work was created to help young people who are not in education, employment or training gain workplace experience, build confidence and prepare for jobs. Participants received practical experience at First Bus’s Rochdale depot alongside support with CVs, applications and interviews.

First Bus said the first programme involved four young people and that two had secured full-time work by October. One joined the engineering stores team at the Rochdale depot, while another found work with Rochdale firm Royton Steelstock.

The local Community Engagement Award recognised a wider year of work with schools, colleges, charities and community groups. First Bus was also shortlisted for Business of the Year at the Rochdale ceremony.

Zoe Hands, managing director of First Bus Franchising, said: “These awards belong to our colleagues and partners, whose passion and commitment help create opportunities for people across Rochdale every day.”

Kevin Mullin, social value manager at First Bus Rochdale, said the recognition reflected the combined work of staff, partners and volunteers supporting local people and strengthening community links.

For Rochdale residents, the award highlights a practical local route into employment for young people who may lack experience or established workplace contacts.

Sources: First Bus Corporate press office, 27 November 2026; UK Bus Awards 2026 results; Rochdale Development Agency.

articles.title: Six arrests made in Middleton over £6 million cannabis importation scheme
articles.excerpt: Authorities arrested six individuals in Middleton as part of a sophisticated cannabis importation plan valued at nearly £6 million, involving a shipment from Canada.
articles.content_html:
Six individuals were arrested in Middleton on Wednesday night in connection with a sophisticated cannabis importation scheme valued at nearly £6 million. The operation involved transporting cannabis concealed within a large lumber shipment from Canada to the UK.

Canadian authorities replaced the cannabis with a synthetic product before it reached the UK. The individuals were observed interacting with the container, which raised suspicions and led to the arrests.

The cannabis was hidden within sophisticated concealments, indicating a well-planned operation.

As investigations continue, authorities are likely to assess the broader implications of this case on local drug-related issues and enforcement strategies.

Police in Canada uncovered the plan and officers there swapped the cannabis — which was hidden with a shipment of timber — for a synthetic product. The shipment was allowed to continue its journey to the UK and was tracked, resulting in officers from Greater Manchester Police’s Serious Organised Crime Group seizing a lorry at an address in Heywood Old Road in Middleton on Wednesday night. GMP said: “Through the strong working relationship developed between our SOCG officers and Canadian law enforcement partners, we were alerted to an attempted import of approximately 590kg of cannabis, which was concealed within a large lumber shipment destined for the UK. “The drugs, worth an estimated street value of £5.9 million, had been hidden within sophisticated concealments inside the shipment. “Canadian authorities successfully seized the cannabis before it left the country, and replaced it with a synthetic substitute. “Following its arrival at docks in Liverpool, we closely monitored the container as it was transported by HGV to an address in Heywood Old Road in Middleton. “Officers maintained surveillance on the shipment and observed a number of individuals interacting with the container. READ MORE: Rise in council staff off with stress and depression “During the unloading process, heavy lifting equipment, including a telescopic handler, was used to remove the cargo.” Five men aged – 32, 43, 45, 48 and 54 – and a woman aged 43, have all been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to import cannabis. They remain in police custody for questioning. Police also recovered a significant amount of suspected Class A drugs at the address. articles.excerpt: Haider Ali has been sentenced to 10 years and six months for his role in an organised crime group supplying class A drugs in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
Haider Ali has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for managing an organised crime group that supplied class A drugs across Rochdale.

The investigation into Ali began after police received information about a drug deal occurring from a car parked on Baron Street in Rochdale town centre just before midnight on 4 January 2025.

Officers followed the vehicle, and when it stopped at a petrol station, they executed a stop to prevent it from fleeing. Ali, a passenger in the car, attempted to walk away but was detained by officers.

During a search, Ali was found with over £1,000 in cash and two mobile phones. Further searches revealed bundles containing heroin and cocaine.

Ali was linked to the Adam drug line and was found to be managing street dealers, having progressed from being a street dealer himself in 2014 to a significant role within the organised crime group by 2024.

Evidence indicated that he directed other dealers on their operations.

The court's decision reflects the serious nature of Ali's crimes and the impact of drug supply on the community. Greater Manchester Police continue to target those involved in drug supply and organised crime to enhance community safety.

articles.title: Six arrested after £5.9m cannabis shipment tracked to Middleton address
articles.excerpt: Six people have been arrested after police tracked a container to Heywood Old Road in Middleton during an international investigation into 590kg of cannabis.
articles.content_html:
Six people have been arrested after police tracked a shipping container to an address on Heywood Old Road in Middleton during an international organised crime investigation.

Greater Manchester Police said the operation concerned about 590kg of cannabis concealed inside a large lumber shipment. Police estimated the drugs would have had a street value of £5.9 million.

According to GMP, Canadian law enforcement officers intercepted the cannabis before it left Canada and replaced it with a synthetic substitute. The container later arrived at docks in Liverpool, where officers began monitoring its journey.

Police said the shipment was transported by HGV to an address on Heywood Old Road on Wednesday 25 November. Officers kept the container under surveillance and watched people interacting with it as cargo was unloaded.

Around 16 pallets were removed using heavy lifting equipment, including a telescopic handler, GMP said. Officers also reported seeing people take photographs and videos of the container and make lengthy telephone calls during the unloading.

Police then entered the address. GMP said officers recovered a significant amount of suspected Class A drugs, although the type, quantity and estimated value were not given in the release.

Five men aged 32, 43, 45, 48 and 54, and a woman aged 43, were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to import cannabis. They remained in police custody for questioning when GMP issued its statement on Thursday 26 November. No charges had been announced.

Detective Inspector Rich McCorry, from GMP's Serious Organised Crime Group, said: "This seizure demonstrates the strength of the relationships we have built with our international law enforcement partners and our continued commitment to tackling organised crime groups operating across international borders.

"Working closely with the Canadian authorities, we were able to identify and disrupt an attempt to flood Greater Manchester's communities with a significant quantity of cannabis worth almost £6 million. I would like to thank our Canadian colleagues for their early notification and assistance with this investigation, without their help we would not have been able to take these drugs off our streets.

"Organised criminal networks often believe they can operate beyond the reach of law enforcement. Operations such as this show that intelligence sharing, partnership working and proactive policing can have a significant impact on criminality both nationally and internationally."

The Heywood Old Road address is in Middleton, within the Rochdale borough. GMP did not report a continuing road closure or public safety warning in connection with the operation.

articles.title: Rochdale Council staff take over 30,000 sick days due to stress and depression
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council staff have taken more than 30,000 sick days due to stress and depression, costing over £4.2 million in sick pay.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council staff have taken more than 30,000 sick days due to stress and depression, costing the authority over £4.2 million in sick pay during the 2025-26 financial year.

The Employment and Equalities Committee will discuss the issue next week, as figures show a total of 30,707.80 sick days were recorded, averaging 11.49 days per full-time employee. This marks an 11.2% increase from the previous year's average of 10.33 days.

The report indicates that 65% of these absences were long-term, while 35% were short-term. The main reasons for long-term absence included stress and depression, alongside operative/post-operative issues and physical injuries.

For short-term absences, stress and depression were again the leading causes, followed by common illnesses such as colds and flu.

The council is actively working to support staff health and wellbeing through various initiatives aimed at preventing ill health and promoting overall wellbeing. These initiatives will be reviewed by the committee to assess their effectiveness.

This averages 11.49 days per full-time employee due to sickness absence, with the main reason being stress/depression — an 11.2% increase on the previous year’s total of 10.33 days. The latest figures show that 65% were long-term absences, 35% were short-term absences and both are consistent with figures for previous years. The report says that the council is continuing to support staff with their health and wellbeing, and is providing a programme of initiatives throughout the year. This includes prevention of ill health and promotion of staff wellbeing. Detailed analysis of the 2025/2026 figures show that the main reasons for long-term absence were stress/depression, operative/post-operative and back and sprains, strains, bruises and breaks. For short-term absences, the reasons are stress/depression, colds/flu/viral infections, diarrhoea/ vomiting/sickness bug. The committee is being asked to note the recommendations in the report, which include monitoring and managing absences to meet annual targets. It adds: “Health and wellbeing is one of the priorities within the council’s people strategy: supporting our workforce to be as well as they can be. READ MORE: Illegal drivers targeted in police operations “The goals for this priority are good health and wellbeing for all employees; staff feel supported in their roles and are resilient; lower sickness levels and reduced staff turnover.” Among further steps to be taken are development of the council’s health and wellbeing action plan, improved communications about wellbeing initiatives, more wellbeing workshops for all staff across multiple locations, working with local organisations to improve access to health and wellbeing offers and providing protected time to staff to access the support/initiatives. As well as staff absences through sickness, the report also shows the council has a 90% staff retention rate, with 2,686 employees retained from a starting workforce of 2,983 for 2025-26. The report adds: “A total of 295 employees left the organisation during the reporting period, of which 239 were voluntary leavers. This equates to a voluntary retention rate of 92.0%. “Retention reporting focuses on voluntary leavers, as these departures provide the most meaningful insight into employee experience and the factors influencing an individual’s decision to remain with or leave the council. “The most common reasons for voluntary leaving were resignation (162 employees; 54.9% of all leavers); normal retirement (50 employees; 16.9%) and early retirement (22 employees; 7.5%).” The council’s retention approach mirrors that of staff wellbeing. The report adds: “The council’s approach to retention focuses on creating an environment where employees feel supported, valued and able to develop their careers. “Retention activity is centred around attracting and welcoming talent through effective recruitment; supporting employee wellbeing; developing careers; and listening and responding through employee engagement activity, staff networks and workforce insight.” The committee meets at 5pm on Wednesday at Number One Riverside. articles.title: Police stop over 100 vehicles in Rochdale and Middleton crackdown on illegal driving
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Police, alongside Trading Standards and DVSA, stopped 118 vehicles in a recent operation targeting illegal drivers in Rochdale and Middleton.
articles.content_html:
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) conducted a significant operation on 25 November 2026, targeting illegal drivers in Rochdale and Middleton, resulting in the stopping of 118 vehicles.

The operation took place at three locations: Mellor Street and Queensway in Rochdale, and Grimshaw Lane in Middleton. Four vehicles were seized for lacking valid insurance, and two individuals were arrested on suspicion of drug-driving and driving while disqualified.

GMP issued 15 Traffic Offence Reports for various violations and conducted five stop-searches under the Misuse of Drugs Act. The operation was prompted by concerns from residents and local councillors about unsafe driving in these areas.

GMP shared that further operations are planned in response to ongoing community concerns about road safety.

articles.title: Campaigners oppose demolition of College Bank flats in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Community leaders are urged to intervene as Rochdale Boroughwide Housing plans to demolish the College Bank flats, citing high refurbishment costs.
articles.content_html:
Campaigners in Rochdale are urging community leaders to intervene against the demolition of the College Bank flats, known as the Seven Sisters.

Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) announced that the demolition and redevelopment of the 61-year-old tower blocks is the only viable option, citing refurbishment costs of at least £269 million and a timeline of up to 12 years.

RBH stated that refurbishing the flats would cost approximately £388,000 for each of the 766 units before VAT, while redevelopment could provide 601 new homes, adding a minimum of 249 bedrooms.

The housing provider claims that the new properties would last significantly longer than the existing flats.

In response to the announcement, the Greater Manchester Tenants Union (GMTU) expressed disappointment, describing the decision as part of a “managed decline” overseen by RBH. GMTU stated, “For 10 years the tenants and leaseholders of College Bank have suffered one mistaken decision after another.”

They criticized RBH for only considering a costly refurbishment plan that includes installing a second staircase in each block, a requirement following the Grenfell disaster.

The decision to demolish them has sparked a strong reaction from the community, with calls for further discussion on the future of the site and the potential impact on local residents.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Campaigners hit out at ‘absurd’ College Bank demolition decision - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Campaigners hit out at ‘absurd’ College Bank demolition decision Campaigners fighting to save Rochdale’s College Bank flats from demolition are calling on community leaders to step in and save the landmark tower blocks. Yesterday, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing announced that demolition and redevelopment of the site is the only viable option for the 61-year-old tower blocks known as the Seven Sisters. It said refurbishing them would cost at least £269 million and take up to 12 years — estimated at £388,000 for each of the 766 flats before VAT. RBH said the renovations would add another 50 years to the lifespan of the buildings, while redevelopment would provide 601 homes in a mix of sizes, creating a minimum additional 249 bedrooms, and the properties would last “significantly longer”. Reacting to the news, Greater Manchester Tenants Union said the decision was part of a “managed decline” overseen by the housing provider — a claim RBH denies. GMTU said: “Campaigners and the wider community are very disappointed with the decision to pursue demolition by RBH. “For 10 years the tenants and leaseholders of College Bank have suffered one mistaken decision after another. “RBH claims the decision is based upon ‘a detailed review of all available scenarios’ but it has only allowed for a costing of an overpriced refurbishment plan based upon installing a second staircase in each block of College Bank (under new regulations following the Grenfell disaster).” The College Bank and Lower Falinge Community Plan to retrofit the iconic tower blocks. Image: College Bank and Lower Falinge Community Plan The union said the demolition of the Seven Sisters would add to the borough’s housing problems. It added: “On March 26, 2012, 13,730 homes were entrusted to RBH from the council. The current stock has been reduced by RBH to a reported 12,276 current total, a loss of 1,434 homes, at this time of severe housing crisis for many families and individuals. “This would be further reduced by 780 homes if we were to lose College Bank, on top of the 140 homes they already want to demolish on neighbouring Lower Falinge, leaving only 11,356 homes — a loss of more than 17 per cent. “The situation in Rochdale is going backwards and while many more people are finding themselves homeless and with temporary accommodation costs rising to £6 million per year, we will lose 920 social-rent homes. “RBH now claims it could replace 780 homes in the Seven Sisters with 601 homes in the same area — a steeply sloped riverbank close to the centre of Rochdale. RBH provided no plans as to how this could be achieved. “Demolition of these homes would be so disruptive, difficult and costly that RBH must demonstrate publicly how this could be more cost effective and socially beneficial than retention before such a plan can be allowed to proceed.” Working with the Save the Seven Sisters campaign group, the union has produced a plan to renovate College Bank and Lower Falinge which it says is more cost effective and less disruptive. READ MORE: Residents’ vision that could create homes for the future The union said: “Greater Manchester Tenants Union has funded the development of a fully costed community plan with architects Unit 38 as an alternative to the loss of these vital social homes during a housing crisis, and the continuing demolitions, displacement and break up of the community, which have massive human and environmental costs. “Andy Burnham said the government is focused on building more social housing and bringing empty homes back into use, a policy prioritised by Mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig, in her manifesto. “If it is serious about wanting to tackle empty homes and increase the supply of social housing, it must intervene to stop this needless waste of social housing and the destruction of our communities. “We call on the political leaders responsible, Paul Waugh MP, Bev Craig and Neil Emmott, to show this absurd and anti-community project up for what it is. We call on them to act, review RBH’s future as responsible for social housing in our borough and take whatever steps are possible to secure the numbers needed to provide safe, warm and dry homes for our community.” Mark Slater, chair of Save the Seven Sisters Campaign, said: “The RBH Board states that given the condition of the buildings, it has a responsibility for the safety for the people that live there. Of course this is true. Paul Roberts, chair of the RBH Board, states that the board ‘has no appetite for the risk’. Greater Manchester Tenants Union protests against demolition plans “What is clear is the condition of the buildings is a result of the neglect and poor management over a number of years by RBH, and there are cost-effective alternatives that could see the blocks refurbished. “The surveys, as presented, would seem to show that there were issues with the fabric of the buildings, but nothing that could not be refurbished. The community that has lived on the estate for the period managed by RBH are clear that since the demolition was proposed in 2016, there has been a policy of managed decline, with RBH consciously running down the blocks and doing the bare minimum. “What is not clear is why RBH has refused to release the surveys for scrutiny and why it will refuse to consider the viable options that would see the Seven Sisters retained in Rochdale with a vibrant community as in years gone by. “If RBH has no appetite to retain social housing in Rochdale, our political representatives must step in and take control of College Bank and Lower Falinge to retain these valuable homes for the community.” Rochdale MP Paul Waugh added: “Paul Waugh said: “This is a sad day for College Bank and for Rochdale. It’s hard to ignore that a lack of investment over many years has contributed to where we are now, and residents have paid the price for that. “I pressed for an independent review of the survey work, and I raised with the Housing Minister whether the blocks could be retrofitted and saved. I’m disappointed that the review has concluded redevelopment is the only viable option. What matters now is that residents get certainty and a real say in what comes next. “RBH has said it will consult residents ahead of a planning application early next year. That consultation needs to be genuine, and it must include tenants who have already been moved out. I also want the council and other providers involved in shaping the future of the site, so that it delivers the good-quality homes Rochdale needs.” READ MORE: Decision made on future of Rochdale’s iconic College Bank towers SUPPORT THE ROCHDALE TIMES: FOLLOW US ON FACEBOOK Got a story?
